prompt: A denim drive converts old denim into environmentally friendly insulation. If 70,000 sq ft of insulation is produced from 36,000 units of denim, how many square feet of insulation can be made from 15,500 units of denim? Express your answer to the nearest whole number.

solutions.title: Unit rate
solutions.body:
Each unit of denim makes $\frac{70}{36} \approx 1.9444$ sq ft. $15{,}500 \times \frac{35}{18} = \frac{542{,}500}{18} \approx 30{,}138.9$.

**Answer: 30,139 sq ft**

prompt: Joseph scored 76, 88, 96 and 98 on his 4 chapter tests this grading period. If the final exam will count twice as much as each of the chapter tests, and the 4 tests and the final exam are the only items contributing to this period's grade, what is the minimum score that Joseph must earn on the final to have an average of 94?

solutions.title: Weighted average
solutions.body:
The final counts as two tests, so there are 6 "test slots": $\frac{76 + 88 + 96 + 98 + 2x}{6} = 94$, so $358 + 2x = 564$, $2x = 206$, $x = 103$.

**Answer: 103**

solutions.title: Balance around 94
solutions.body:
Differences from 94: $-18, -6, +2, +4$, total $-18$. The final, counting twice, must make up $+18$, i.e. $+9$ each time: $94 + 9 = 103$.

**Answer: 103**

prompt: The final exam scores earned by the 16 students in Joseph's class are as follows: 80, 79, 96, 93, 94, 92, 88, 87, 90, 81, 83, 82, 89, 99, 91, 73. What is the positive difference between the median of these scores and the average (arithmetic mean) of these scores? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest hundredth.

solutions.title: Deviations from 88.5
solutions.body:
Subtract 88.5 from each score and add: the total is $1397 - 16(88.5) = 1397 - 1416 = -19$. So the mean is $88.5 - \frac{19}{16} = 88.5 - 1.1875$, and the difference is $1.1875 \approx 1.19$.

**Answer: 1.19**

prompt: In another one of Joseph's classes the 14 8th graders averaged 94 on the final exam, while the 12 7th graders averaged 89 on the final exam. What was the average score for the entire class? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest hundredth.

solutions.title: Weighted from 89
solutions.body:
The 8th graders are 5 points above 89, and they are $\frac{14}{26}$ of the class: $89 + 5 \cdot \frac{14}{26} = 89 + \frac{70}{26} \approx 89 + 2.692 = 91.69$.

**Answer: 91.69**

prompt: At Walter Whitman Middle School, to celebrate the last day of school, Mrs. Hanks brought in treats for her class. She has chocolate bars, lollipops and gumballs. Mrs. Hanks tells each student they can choose any combination of three treats from what she has. How many different combinations of three treats can one of her students choose?

solutions.title: List by type
solutions.body:
Call the treats A, B, C.
- All different: ABC — 1.
- All the same: AAA, BBB, CCC — 3.
- Two of one, one of another: AAB, AAC, BBA, BBC, CCA, CCB — 6.

Total $1 + 3 + 6 = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

solutions.title: Stars and bars
solutions.body:
Choosing 3 treats from 3 types with repetition allowed: $\binom{3 + 3 - 1}{3} = \binom53 = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

prompt: At the end-of-year assembly, WWMS holds a raffle, in which several lucky students will each win a gift certificate to the famous Giorgio's Gelato. There are 10 gift certificates to be raffled to the 6th graders, 15 gift certificates to be raffled to the 7th graders and 20 gift certificates to be raffled to the 8th graders. Each grade has 300 students. Junie is in 8th grade at WWMS. Junie's sister and brother also attend WWMS and are in 7th and 6th grade, respectively. What is the probability that at least one of the three siblings wins a gift certificate? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Complement
solutions.body:
Each grade's certificates go to different students, so the 6th-grade brother wins with probability $\frac{10}{300} = \frac1{30}$, the 7th-grade sister with $\frac{15}{300} = \frac1{20}$, and Junie with $\frac{20}{300} = \frac1{15}$. The three raffles are separate, so the events are independent.

$P(\text{nobody wins}) = \frac{29}{30} \cdot \frac{19}{20} \cdot \frac{14}{15} = \frac{7714}{9000}$.

$P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - \frac{7714}{9000} = \frac{1286}{9000} = \frac{643}{4500} \approx 0.143$.

(Simply adding $\frac1{30} + \frac1{20} + \frac1{15} = \frac{3}{20}$ counts the cases where two or three of them win more than once.)

**Answer: $\frac{643}{4500}$**

reviewNote: The official solution gives 3/20 by adding 1/30 + 1/20 + 1/15, which double-counts outcomes where two or three siblings win (the events are not mutually exclusive). The correct probability 1 - (29/30)(19/20)(14/15) = 643/4500 is used here; a human should confirm.

prompt: Before WWMS students were officially released for summer vacation, the staff had to conduct an official check of all 900 lockers, numbered from 1 to 900. Once the locker check was completed, all 900 lockers remained open. As students exited in an orderly fashion, walking down the hallway single file, the 1st student closed all the lockers. The 2nd student then opened every even numbered locker. The 3rd student changed the status of every locker whose number was a multiple of three – opened it if closed or closed it if opened. The 4th student then did the same for every locker whose number was a multiple of four, and so on through the 900th student who changed the status of locker number 900. When all of the students had left the school, how many lockers were closed?

solutions.title: Count the toggles
solutions.body:
Locker $n$ is toggled once by each student whose number divides $n$. Starting open, it ends closed after an odd number of toggles, i.e. when $n$ has an odd number of divisors. Divisors pair up ($d$ with $n/d$) except when $d = n/d$, so only perfect squares have an odd number of divisors. The squares from 1 to 900 are $1^2, 2^2, \dots, 30^2$: **30** lockers.

**Answer: 30**

solutions.title: Small case check
solutions.body:
Try lockers 1–10: locker 1 (divisor 1) closed; 2 (1,2) open; 3 open; 4 (1,2,4) closed; 5–8 open; 9 (1,3,9) closed; 10 open. Closed lockers are 1, 4, 9 — the squares. Up to 900 there are 30 squares.

**Answer: 30**

prompt: Summer Fun Camp enrollment costs 85 dollars each week per camper. Each camper may register for up to three of the optional workshops offered for an additional charge of \$5.50 a week per workshop, or 15 dollars per week for three workshops. The total charge for Chloe's enrollment to attend Summer Fun Camp for $n$ weeks this summer is 768 dollars. If Chloe has registered to participate in two workshops each week, what is the value of $n$?

solutions.title: Weekly cost
solutions.body:
Each week costs $85 + 2(5.50) = 96$ dollars. $96n = 768$, so $n = 8$.

**Answer: 8**

prompt: Summer Fun Camp enrollment costs 85 dollars each week per camper. Each camper may register for up to three of the optional workshops offered for an additional charge of \$5.50 a week per workshop, or 15 dollars per week for three workshops. This summer, Lailan will attend Summer Fun Camp for six weeks and participate in the soccer, band and cheerleading workshops. If Lailan registered to participate in these three workshops each week, what is her total charge for six weeks of Summer Fun Camp and workshops?

solutions.title: Per week
solutions.body:
Each week: $85 + 15 = 100$ dollars (three workshops cost the 15-dollar package price, cheaper than $3 \times 5.50 = 16.50$). Six weeks: $600$ dollars.

**Answer: 600 dollars**

solutions.title: Separate totals
solutions.body:
Camp: $85 \times 6 = 510$. Workshops: $15 \times 6 = 90$. Total $600$.

**Answer: 600 dollars**

prompt: Summer Fun Camp enrollment costs 85 dollars each week per camper. Each camper may register for up to three of the optional workshops offered for an additional charge of \$5.50 a week per workshop, or 15 dollars per week for three workshops. Lailan will attend Summer Fun Camp for six weeks with the three-workshop package each week. This summer, Ailee plans to attend three different camps – a two-week soccer camp, followed by a two-week band camp, followed by a two-week cheerleading camp. The total cost for Ailee's band camp enrollment is 100 dollars more than the total cost of her soccer camp enrollment, and the total cost of her cheerleading camp enrollment is one-fourth the combined total costs for her enrollment in all three camps. If the combined total costs for Ailee's enrollment in all three camps is equal to Lailan's total charge for six weeks of Summer Fun Camp and workshops, what is the total cost of Ailee's band camp enrollment?

solutions.title: Set up equations
solutions.body:
Lailan pays $6(85 + 15) = 600$ dollars, so Ailee's camps total $s + b + c = 600$. Cheerleading is one-fourth: $c = 150$, so $s + b = 450$. With $b = s + 100$: $2s + 100 = 450$, $s = 175$, $b = 275$.

**Answer: 275 dollars**

solutions.title: Half-difference trick
solutions.body:
Soccer and band together cost $600 - \frac14(600) = 450$ and differ by 100. The larger is $\frac{450 + 100}{2} = 275$.

**Answer: 275 dollars**

prompt: A stand at a local parade is selling flags for observers to wave. The small flags each cost $\frac23$ the price of each large flag, and each flag costs a whole number of dollars. If Frida bought 5 flags and spent \$24.00, how much do each of the small flags cost in dollars?

solutions.title: Guess and check
solutions.body:
The large price must be a multiple of 3. Try large \$6, small \$4: three small and two large cost $12 + 12 = 24$ ✓. (Large \$3/small \$2 gives at most \$15; large \$9/small \$6 gives at least \$30.)

**Answer: \$4**

solutions.title: Algebra
solutions.body:
Let large $= 3k$, small $= 2k$, with $a$ small and $5 - a$ large: $2ka + 3k(5 - a) = 24$, so $k(15 - a) = 24$. With $0 \le a \le 5$, $15 - a$ is between 10 and 15 and divides 24 only for $15 - a = 12$: $a = 3$, $k = 2$. Small flags cost $2k = 4$.

**Answer: \$4**

prompt: The American flag has 13 horizontal stripes of equal height. If the flag outside of Victor's house is 4 feet tall and 6 feet wide, how many inches tall is each of the 13 stripes? Express your answer as a mixed number.

solutions.title: Convert, then divide
solutions.body:
4 ft $= 48$ in. $48 \div 13 = 3\frac{9}{13}$ in.

**Answer: $3\frac{9}{13}$ inches**

solutions.title: Long division
solutions.body:
$13 \times 3 = 39$, remainder $48 - 39 = 9$, so $\frac{48}{13} = 3\frac{9}{13}$.

**Answer: $3\frac{9}{13}$ inches**

prompt: On a bright, sunny day, Janine is standing 6 feet 3 inches away from the base of a 20-foot-tall flagpole. She notices that her shadow just touches the base of the flagpole. If Janine is exactly 5 feet tall, how long is the shadow of the flagpole at this same time?

solutions.title: Similar triangles
solutions.body:
Janine's shadow is 6 ft 3 in $= 6.25$ ft long. Shadows are proportional to heights: $\frac{6.25}{5} = \frac{x}{20}$, so $x = 25$ ft.

**Answer: 25 feet**

solutions.title: Shadow ratio
solutions.body:
Her shadow is $6.25 \div 5 = 1.25$ times her height, so the pole's shadow is $1.25 \times 20 = 25$ ft.

**Answer: 25 feet**

prompt: Small Town Ice Cream Shoppe carries five kinds of ice cream: vanilla, chocolate, strawberry, lemon custard and caramel swirl. They also have three types of toppings: sprinkles, chopped nuts and hot fudge. A "Shoppe Supreme" consists of three scoops of ice cream, not necessarily distinct flavors, and three scoops of toppings, also not necessarily distinct. If the ice cream is always scooped before the toppings are added, in how many distinct ways can a Shoppe Supreme be assembled at the Small Town Ice Cream Shoppe?

solutions.title: Multiplication principle
solutions.body:
The six scoops are added in order. Each ice cream scoop has 5 choices and each topping scoop has 3 choices: $5^3 \times 3^3 = 125 \times 27 = 3375$ ways of assembling.

**Answer: 3375**

solutions.title: Same idea, grouped
solutions.body:
Ice cream sequences: $5 \cdot 5 \cdot 5 = 125$. Topping sequences: $3 \cdot 3 \cdot 3 = 27$. Each pair gives a different assembly: $125 \times 27 = 3375$. Equivalently, $(5 \times 3)^3 = 15^3 = 3375$.

**Answer: 3375**

prompt: In the Ice Cream Shoppe, there are stools at the counter. Janet, Mason, Renae, Steve and Trina are going to sit side-by-side at the counter so that there are no empty seats between them. If Trina and Mason must sit next to each other, in how many possible distinct orders can they sit?

solutions.title: Treat the pair as one
solutions.body:
Glue Trina and Mason into one unit: 4 units can be ordered in $4! = 24$ ways, and the pair can be TM or MT: $24 \times 2 = 48$.

**Answer: 48**

solutions.title: Place the pair
solutions.body:
The adjacent pair occupies seats 1-2, 2-3, 3-4 or 4-5 (4 choices), in 2 orders, and the other 3 people fill the remaining seats in $3! = 6$ ways: $4 \times 2 \times 6 = 48$.

**Answer: 48**

prompt: Janet, Mason, Renae, Steve and Trina each ordered a different drink, but the waitress has forgotten who ordered what (and she is too embarrassed to ask). If she randomly places the drinks down, one in front of each person, what is the probability that she sets each of the five drinks down in front of the person who ordered it? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: One correct arrangement
solutions.body:
There are $5! = 120$ equally likely ways to hand out the drinks, and exactly one is fully correct: $\frac{1}{120}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{120}$**

solutions.title: Drink by drink
solutions.body:
First drink correct: $\frac15$; then $\frac14$, $\frac13$, $\frac12$, $1$. Product: $\frac{1}{120}$.

**Answer: $\frac{1}{120}$**

prompt: While walking around at their town's Independence Day Festival, Latrease and Hannah decide to buy lunch. Latrease bought two hot dogs and a soda for a total of \$7.50. Hannah bought a hot dog, a soda, and a bag of chips for \$5.50. If a bag of chips costs \$1.00, how much does one hot dog cost?

solutions.title: Subtract the orders
solutions.body:
Hannah's hot dog and soda cost $5.50 - 1.00 = 4.50$. Latrease's order has one more hot dog: $7.50 - 4.50 = 3.00$.

**Answer: \$3.00**

prompt: Frank is going to put on a fireworks show for his neighborhood. He bought 15 different fireworks to set off. If he plans to end with a specific sequence of five fireworks and he only wants to set off one firework at a time, how many distinct orders are there in which he could set off the fireworks?

solutions.title: Only the first ten vary
solutions.body:
The last five are fixed, so only the other 10 fireworks can be arranged in the first 10 slots: $10! = 3{,}628{,}800$.

**Answer: 3,628,800**

solutions.title: Slot by slot
solutions.body:
Slot 1 has 10 choices, slot 2 has 9, …, slot 10 has 1, and slots 11–15 have 1 each: $10 \cdot 9 \cdots 1 = 3{,}628{,}800$.

**Answer: 3,628,800**

prompt: Victoria and Hugo bought 42 cups of lemonade for the 10 guests they expected to have at their 4th of July party plus themselves. If 13 guests end up coming to the party, what is the minimum number of additional cups of lemonade that Victoria and Hugo must buy in order to have the planned amount of lemonade available to each guest and themselves? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest tenth.

solutions.title: Cups per person
solutions.body:
Planned: $42 \div 12 = 3.5$ cups per person. 3 extra guests need $3 \times 3.5 = 10.5$ more cups.

**Answer: 10.5 cups**

solutions.title: New total
solutions.body:
15 people at 3.5 cups is $52.5$ cups; they have 42, so they need $10.5$ more.

**Answer: 10.5 cups**

prompt: According to the ruler, how many centimeters long is the piece of washi tape shown here?

solutions.title: Read both ends
solutions.body:
The left end of the tape lines up with the 12 cm mark and the right end lines up with the 24 cm mark. The length is $24 - 12 = 12$ cm.

**Answer: 12 cm**

solutions.title: Count the centimeters
solutions.body:
Count the big tick marks covered by the tape: from 12 to 13, 13 to 14, …, 23 to 24. That is 12 one-centimeter steps.

**Answer: 12 cm**

prompt:
What is the tens digit of this sum?

$$\begin{array}{r} 12{,}345 \\ +\ 56{,}789 \\ \hline \end{array}$$

solutions.title: Only the last two digits matter
solutions.body:
The tens digit depends only on the last two digits: $45 + 89 = 134$, whose tens digit is 3.

**Answer: 3**

prompt: Dora drinks a 12-ounce can of cola. Erika drinks half of a 20-ounce bottle of cola. How many more ounces of cola does Dora drink than Erika?

solutions.title: Compute
solutions.body:
Erika drinks $20 \div 2 = 10$ ounces. Dora drinks $12 - 10 = 2$ more ounces.

**Answer: 2 ounces**

prompt: What is the result when one hundred twenty-eight thousand is subtracted from one million?

solutions.title: Work in thousands
solutions.body:
One million is 1000 thousands. $1000 - 128 = 872$ thousands, i.e. $872{,}000$.

**Answer: 872,000**

prompt: What is the side length of a rectangle that has width 7 inches and area 105 in$^2$?

solutions.title: Divide the area
solutions.body:
Area = length × width, so length $= 105 \div 7 = 15$ inches.

**Answer: 15 inches**

prompt: What integer is closest to $-7\pi$?

solutions.title: Estimate
solutions.body:
$\pi \approx 3.1416$, so $7\pi \approx 21.99$ and $-7\pi \approx -21.99$. The closest integer is $-22$.

**Answer: −22**

solutions.title: Bound it
solutions.body:
$3.14 < \pi < 3.15$ gives $21.98 < 7\pi < 22.05$, so $7\pi$ is within $0.05$ of 22, and $-7\pi$ is closest to $-22$.

**Answer: −22**

prompt: On Monday at 8 p.m., the temperature measured −17 degrees. Between 8 p.m. on Monday and 6 a.m. on Tuesday, the temperature increased 23 degrees. On Tuesday, between 6 a.m. and 3 p.m., the temperature decreased 5 degrees. What was the temperature on Tuesday at 3 p.m.?

solutions.title: Step by step
solutions.body:
$-17 + 23 = 6$ degrees at 6 a.m. Then $6 - 5 = 1$ degree at 3 p.m.

**Answer: 1 degree**

solutions.title: Net change
solutions.body:
The net change is $+23 - 5 = +18$ degrees, so the final temperature is $-17 + 18 = 1$ degree.

**Answer: 1 degree**

prompt: This table shows all five lunch options on Friday at a middle school and the number of students that ordered each. Based on this, what percent of the lunch orders on Friday were for spaghetti?

solutions.title: Scale to 100
solutions.body:
400 orders is 4 groups of 100; $44 \div 4 = 11$ spaghetti orders per 100 orders, so 11%.

**Answer: 11%**

prompt: What is the 40th positive odd integer?

solutions.title: Formula
solutions.body:
The $n$th positive odd integer is $2n - 1$. For $n = 40$: $2 \cdot 40 - 1 = 79$.

**Answer: 79**

solutions.title: Pair with even numbers
solutions.body:
The 40th positive even integer is 80; each odd integer is 1 less than the even integer in the same position, so the 40th odd integer is 79.

**Answer: 79**

prompt: What is the value of the expression $1 + \dfrac{2}{1 - \frac{2}{3}}$, in simplest form?
If $(x^2y^3)^2 = x^ay^b$, what is the value of $a + b$?

solutions.title: Shortcut
solutions.body:
Squaring doubles every exponent, so $a + b = 2(2 + 3) = 10$.

**Answer: 10**

prompt: For each rock-paper-scissors match, paper beats rock, rock beats scissors, scissors beat paper and two identical items result in a tie. Based on this table, which summarizes the results of Kalyani and Mark’s last 200 matches, how many matches did Kalyani win?

solutions.title: Find the winning cells
solutions.body:
Columns are Kalyani’s choice and rows are Mark’s. Kalyani wins when:
- Kalyani paper, Mark rock: 24
- Kalyani rock, Mark scissors: 20
- Kalyani scissors, Mark paper: 21

Total: $24 + 20 + 21 = 65$.

**Answer: 65 matches**

solutions.title: Subtract ties and losses
solutions.body:
Ties (diagonal): $30 + 21 + 18 = 69$. Mark wins (Mark rock vs scissors 20, Mark paper vs rock 26, Mark scissors vs paper 20): 66. Kalyani wins $200 - 69 - 66 = 65$.

**Answer: 65 matches**

prompt: Given that a mile equals 5280 feet, how many inches are in one-sixth of a mile?

solutions.title: Feet first
solutions.body:
One-sixth of a mile is $5280 \div 6 = 880$ feet, which is $880 \times 12 = 10{,}560$ inches.

**Answer: 10,560 inches**

solutions.title: Simplify first
solutions.body:
$\frac{5280 \times 12}{6} = 5280 \times 2 = 10{,}560$ inches.

**Answer: 10,560 inches**

prompt: Maria was born on January 1, 2000. Her mother was born on January 1, 1975 and her father was born on January 1, 1970. In what year was the sum of their ages 100?

solutions.title: Equation
solutions.body:
In year $Y$ the ages are $Y - 2000$, $Y - 1975$, $Y - 1970$. Their sum is $3Y - 5945 = 100$, so $3Y = 6045$ and $Y = 2015$.

**Answer: 2015**

solutions.title: Start in 2000
solutions.body:
On January 1, 2000 the ages are 0, 25 and 30, sum 55. Each year adds 3 to the sum, and we need $100 - 55 = 45$ more, i.e. 15 years: 2015.

**Answer: 2015**

prompt: A bicycle that originally cost \$200 is on sale for \$140. By what percent was the price reduced?

solutions.title: Percent decrease
solutions.body:
The reduction is $200 - 140 = 60$ dollars, and $\frac{60}{200} = 30\%$.

**Answer: 30%**

solutions.title: Compare prices
solutions.body:
$\frac{140}{200} = 70\%$ of the original price, so the price was reduced by $100\% - 70\% = 30\%$.

**Answer: 30%**

prompt: Jay’s dog outgrew his rectangular pen that measured 10 feet by 14 feet. To make it larger, he increased each side length by the same amount, which increased the pen’s area by 81 square feet. What is the greater side length of the larger pen?

solutions.title: Look for factors
solutions.body:
The new area is $140 + 81 = 221$ sq ft, and the new sides differ by 4. Since $221 = 13 \times 17$, the new pen is 13 ft by 17 ft.

**Answer: 17 feet**

solutions.title: Equation
solutions.body:
Let $x$ be the increase: $(10 + x)(14 + x) = 221$, so $x^2 + 24x - 81 = 0$, $(x + 27)(x - 3) = 0$, $x = 3$. The greater side is $14 + 3 = 17$ ft.

**Answer: 17 feet**

prompt: Parker has three sons: Alfred, Beto and Dell. When Alfred turned 11 years old, Beto was 9 years old and Dell was 4 years old. What was the average of their ages when Alfred turned 37?

solutions.title: Find each age
solutions.body:
Alfred aged $37 - 11 = 26$ years, so Beto is $9 + 26 = 35$ and Dell is $4 + 26 = 30$. Average: $\frac{37 + 35 + 30}{3} = \frac{102}{3} = 34$.

**Answer: 34 years**

solutions.title: Shift the average
solutions.body:
The average was $\frac{11 + 9 + 4}{3} = 8$. Everyone is 26 years older, so the average is $8 + 26 = 34$.

**Answer: 34 years**

prompt: Triangle $ABC$ has an area of 40 units$^2$. Point $D$ is on side $AC$, and $AD:DC = 3:1$. What is the area of triangle $BDC$?

solutions.title: Same height
solutions.body:
Triangles $ABD$ and $BDC$ share the height from $B$ to line $AC$, so their areas are in the ratio of their bases $3:1$. Triangle $BDC$ gets $\frac14$ of 40, which is 10.

**Answer: 10 units²**

solutions.title: Formula
solutions.body:
Area of $BDC = \frac12 \cdot DC \cdot h = \frac12 \cdot \frac{AC}{4} \cdot h = \frac14 \left(\frac12 \cdot AC \cdot h\right) = \frac{40}{4} = 10$.

**Answer: 10 units²**

prompt: Kendra surveyed 100 people who own a dog or a cat, or both. Of those surveyed, 15 own both a dog and a cat, and the number of people who own a dog is four times the number of people who own a cat. How many people surveyed own a cat?

solutions.title: Inclusion–exclusion
solutions.body:
Let $c$ own a cat, so $4c$ own a dog. Then $4c + c - 15 = 100$, so $5c = 115$ and $c = 23$.

**Answer: 23 people**

solutions.title: Check with a Venn diagram
solutions.body:
With 23 cat owners and 92 dog owners: cat only $23 - 15 = 8$, dog only $92 - 15 = 77$, both 15. Total $8 + 77 + 15 = 100$ ✓.

**Answer: 23 people**

prompt: What is the area of the region in the first quadrant that lies between the lines $x + 3y = 12$ and $x + 3y = 18$?

solutions.title: Subtract triangles
solutions.body:
Each line cuts off a right triangle with the axes. $x + 3y = 18$ meets the axes at $(18, 0)$ and $(0, 6)$: area $\frac12 \cdot 18 \cdot 6 = 54$. $x + 3y = 12$ meets them at $(12, 0)$ and $(0, 4)$: area $\frac12 \cdot 12 \cdot 4 = 24$. The region between them has area $54 - 24 = 30$.

**Answer: 30 units²**

solutions.title: Similar triangles
solutions.body:
The two triangles are similar with ratio $12 : 18 = 2 : 3$, so their areas are in ratio $4 : 9$. The big one has area 54, the small one $\frac49 \cdot 54 = 24$, and the difference is 30.

**Answer: 30 units²**

prompt: What is the absolute difference between the mean and median of the first 100 positive integers?

solutions.title: Compute both
solutions.body:
Mean: $\frac{1 + 2 + \cdots + 100}{100} = \frac{5050}{100} = 50.5$. Median: average of the 50th and 51st values, $\frac{50 + 51}{2} = 50.5$. Difference: 0.

**Answer: 0**

solutions.title: Symmetry
solutions.body:
The numbers $1, \dots, 100$ are symmetric about $50.5$, so both the mean and the median equal $50.5$.

**Answer: 0**

prompt: The square labeled A has area 81 units$^2$. The square labeled B has area 16 units$^2$. The square labeled C has area 36 units$^2$. These three squares along with the shaded, non-overlapping rectangles labeled D, E and F are arranged to form a large square as shown. What is the area of rectangle D?

solutions.title: Find the side lengths
solutions.body:
The squares have sides 9 (A), 4 (B) and 6 (C). The bottom edge of the large square is A plus C: $9 + 6 = 15$, so the large square has side 15.

- D sits on top of A, so its height is $15 - 9 = 6$.
- B and F together span the width of C (6), so F has width $6 - 4 = 2$, and D spans A plus F: width $9 + 2 = 11$.

Area of D $= 11 \times 6 = 66$.

**Answer: 66 units²**

solutions.title: Subtract from the whole
solutions.body:
The large square (side 15) has area 225. The right column (width 6) has C (height 6) at the bottom, B (height 4) above it, and E on top with the same width as B: E is $4 \times (15 - 6 - 4) = 4 \times 5 = 20$. F fills the gap between the top of C (height 6) and the top of A (height 9) next to B: $2 \times 3 = 6$. So D $= 225 - 81 - 16 - 36 - 20 - 6 = 66$.

**Answer: 66 units²**

prompt: If a fair coin is tossed four times, what is the probability of it landing heads up at least three times? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Count outcomes
solutions.body:
There are $2^4 = 16$ equally likely outcomes. Exactly 3 heads: $\binom43 = 4$ outcomes; 4 heads: 1 outcome. Probability $\frac{5}{16}$.

**Answer: $\frac{5}{16}$**

solutions.title: List them
solutions.body:
HHHH, HHHT, HHTH, HTHH, THHH — 5 of the 16 sequences.

**Answer: $\frac{5}{16}$**

prompt: If $n$ is an integer for which the greatest common factor of $n$ and 18 is 6 and the least common multiple of $n$ and 9 is 126, what is the value of $n$?

solutions.title: Prime factorizations
solutions.body:
$126 = 2 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 7$ and $9 = 3^2$, so $n$ must contain $2 \cdot 7$ and at most $3^2$. Since $\gcd(n, 18) = 6 = 2 \cdot 3$, $n$ has exactly one factor of 3 (two would make the GCF 18). So $n = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7 = 42$.

**Answer: 42**

solutions.title: Check divisors of 126
solutions.body:
$n$ divides 126 and is a multiple of 6: candidates 6, 18, 42, 126. $\text{lcm}(6,9) = 18$, $\gcd(18,18) = 18$, $\gcd(126, 18) = 18$; only 42 works: $\gcd(42,18) = 6$, $\text{lcm}(42,9) = 126$.

**Answer: 42**

prompt: The lines given by the equations $y = 9 - \frac13 x$ and $y = mx + b$ are perpendicular and intersect at a point on the $x$-axis. What is the value of $b$?

solutions.title: Slope and point
solutions.body:
The first line has slope $-\frac13$, so $m = 3$. It meets the $x$-axis where $0 = 9 - \frac{x}{3}$, i.e. $x = 27$. The second line passes through $(27, 0)$: $0 = 3 \cdot 27 + b$, so $b = -81$.

**Answer: −81**

solutions.title: Point-slope form
solutions.body:
The second line is $y = 3(x - 27) = 3x - 81$, so $b = -81$.

**Answer: −81**

prompt: If two standard, fair 6-sided dice are rolled, what is the probability that the product of the two numbers rolled is a perfect square? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Doubles plus extras
solutions.body:
All 6 doubles give squares. Otherwise the two numbers must have the same square-free part; among 1–6 only 1 and 4 share one. That adds (1,4) and (4,1): $\frac{8}{36} = \frac29$.

**Answer: $\frac{2}{9}$**

prompt: Gracie has made 2 gallons of punch that contains 50% juice. After Gracie pours out some of her mixture and replaces it with an equal amount of pure 100% juice, she has 2 gallons of punch that contains 65% juice. How many gallons of the original mixture did Gracie pour out? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Track the juice
solutions.body:
Let $x$ gallons be replaced. Juice: $1 - 0.5x + x = 0.65 \cdot 2 = 1.3$, so $0.5x = 0.3$ and $x = \frac35$.

**Answer: $\frac35$ gallon**

solutions.title: Track the water
solutions.body:
Water starts at 1 gallon and must end at $0.35 \cdot 2 = 0.7$ gallon. Each gallon poured out removes 0.5 gallon of water, so she removes $\frac{0.3}{0.5} = \frac35$ gallon.

**Answer: $\frac35$ gallon**

prompt: Ursula’s starting location (green plus sign) is on the shore of a river that measures 8 km across. Her destination (red X) is 27 km downshore on the opposite side of the river. Ursula rows a boat in a straight line, at a speed of 5 km/h, to a point that is 6 km downshore on the opposite side, and then runs the remaining distance, at a speed of 14 km/h. How many hours will it take Ursula to reach her destination? Express your answer as a mixed number.

solutions.title: Pythagorean theorem
solutions.body:
The rowing path is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 and 6: $\sqrt{64 + 36} = 10$ km, taking $10 \div 5 = 2$ hours. She then runs $27 - 6 = 21$ km, taking $21 \div 14 = 1\frac12$ hours. Total: $3\frac12$ hours.

**Answer: $3\frac12$ hours**

prompt: A cylinder whose height is 3 times its radius is inscribed in a cone whose height is 6 times its radius. What fraction of the cone’s volume lies inside the cylinder? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Similar triangles
solutions.body:
Let the cone have radius $R$ and height $6R$, and the cylinder radius $r$ and height $3r$. Above the cylinder is a small cone similar to the big one, with radius $r$ and height $6R - 3r$. Its height is 6 times its radius: $6R - 3r = 6r$, so $r = \frac23R$ and the cylinder’s height is $2R$.

Cylinder: $\pi r^2 h = \pi \cdot \frac49R^2 \cdot 2R = \frac89\pi R^3$. Cone: $\frac13\pi R^2 \cdot 6R = 2\pi R^3$. Ratio: $\frac{8/9}{2} = \frac49$.

**Answer: $\frac{4}{9}$**

solutions.title: Pick numbers
solutions.body:
Take $R = 3$: cone height 18. The cylinder’s top rim lies on the cone’s side, where the radius at height $h$ is $3 - \frac{h}{6}$. With radius $r$ at height $3r$: $r = 3 - \frac{r}{2}$, so $r = 2$, height 6. Volumes: cylinder $\pi \cdot 4 \cdot 6 = 24\pi$, cone $\frac13 \pi \cdot 9 \cdot 18 = 54\pi$. Ratio $\frac{24}{54} = \frac49$.

**Answer: $\frac{4}{9}$**

prompt: What value of $x$ yields the minimum value of the sum $|x - 2^0| + |x - 2^1| + |x - 2^2| + |x - 2^3| + \cdots + |x - 2^{10}|$?

solutions.title: Median minimizes distance
solutions.body:
The sum of distances from $x$ to a list of points is smallest at the median of the points. The 11 points $2^0, 2^1, \dots, 2^{10}$ have median $2^5 = 32$.

**Answer: 32**

solutions.title: Pair the terms
solutions.body:
Pair $|x - 2^0| + |x - 2^{10}|$, $|x - 2^1| + |x - 2^9|$, …, $|x - 2^4| + |x - 2^6|$. Each pair is at least the distance between its two points, with equality when $x$ lies between them; all pairs achieve that for $2^4 \le x \le 2^6$. The leftover term $|x - 2^5|$ is smallest (0) at $x = 32$, which lies in that range.

**Answer: 32**

prompt: Charles has opened a service, called Charlie’s Chores, that performs various household chores for families in his neighborhood. The table shows the amount he charges for each chore and how many times he was hired to complete that chore in January. How much money in dollars did Charlie’s Chores earn in the month of January?

solutions.title: Multiply and add
solutions.body:
- Ironing: $10 \times 9.50 = 95$
- Dog walking: $12 \times 7.50 = 90$
- Kitchen cleaning: $7 \times 12 = 84$
- Snow shoveling: $5 \times 14 = 70$

Total: $95 + 90 + 84 + 70 = 339$ dollars.

**Answer: \$339**

prompt: Sunil draws a regular hexagon and a convex quadrilateral on a sheet of paper, so that no side of the quadrilateral lies on the same line as a side of the hexagon. What is the maximum total number of points in which the sides of the quadrilateral can intersect the sides of the hexagon?

solutions.title: Bound each side
solutions.body:
A line segment can cross the boundary of a convex polygon at most twice (once going in, once going out). The quadrilateral has 4 sides, so there are at most $4 \times 2 = 8$ intersection points. Eight is achievable: draw a square with the same center as the hexagon, with its corners just outside the hexagon but the midpoints of its sides inside it (for a hexagon with vertices at distance 1 from the center, a square with corners at distance 0.99 from the center works, as long as no corner points at a hexagon vertex). Each side of the square starts outside, passes through the hexagon and leaves again, crossing it twice.

**Answer: 8 points**

prompt: Penelope and George go trick-or-treating together. Penelope gets 152 pieces of candy and George gets 124 pieces of candy. Penelope eats 5 pieces of candy every day, and George eats 4 pieces of candy every day. After how many days will George have the same amount of candy as Penelope?

solutions.title: Close the gap
solutions.body:
Penelope starts with $152 - 124 = 28$ more pieces, and the gap shrinks by $5 - 4 = 1$ piece per day. It closes after 28 days (both then have $152 - 140 = 12 = 124 - 112$ pieces).

**Answer: 28 days**

solutions.title: Equation
solutions.body:
$152 - 5d = 124 - 4d \Rightarrow d = 28$.

**Answer: 28 days**

prompt: Rosie grows 160 bushels of corn per acre in a right triangular field, as shown, with perpendicular sides of lengths 660 feet and 1320 feet. Given that an acre equals 43,560 ft$^2$, what is the total number of bushels of corn that Rosie grows?

solutions.title: Area in acres
solutions.body:
Area $= \frac12 \cdot 660 \cdot 1320 = 435{,}600$ ft², which is $435{,}600 \div 43{,}560 = 10$ acres. Bushels: $10 \times 160 = 1600$.

**Answer: 1600 bushels**

prompt: A standard, six-sided die is rolled five times. What is the probability that the five rolls are either all the same or all different? Express your answer to the nearest hundredth of a percent.

solutions.title: Count outcomes
solutions.body:
Total outcomes: $6^5 = 7776$. All the same: 6. All different: $6 \cdot 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 = 720$. Probability $\frac{726}{7776} \approx 0.093364$, i.e. $9.34\%$.

**Answer: 9.34%**

solutions.title: Multiply probabilities
solutions.body:
All same: $\left(\frac16\right)^4 \approx 0.000772$. All different: $\frac56 \cdot \frac46 \cdot \frac36 \cdot \frac26 \approx 0.092593$. Sum $\approx 0.093364 = 9.34\%$.

**Answer: 9.34%**

prompt: If $(0, 0)$, $(6, 2)$, $(-2, 6)$ and $(a, b)$ are the coordinates of the vertices of a parallelogram, what is the least possible value for $a + b$?

solutions.title: Three possible fourth vertices
solutions.body:
In a parallelogram the fourth vertex equals the sum of its two neighbors minus the opposite vertex. Choosing each given point as the one opposite $(a, b)$:
- $(6,2) + (-2,6) - (0,0) = (4, 8)$, sum 12
- $(0,0) + (6,2) - (-2,6) = (8, -4)$, sum 4
- $(0,0) + (-2,6) - (6,2) = (-8, 4)$, sum $-4$

The least value is $-4$.

**Answer: −4**

solutions.title: Shortcut with sums
solutions.body:
Let $s$ be the coordinate sum: the points have $s = 0, 8, 4$. The fourth vertex’s sum is (sum of two) − (third): $8 + 4 - 0 = 12$, $0 + 8 - 4 = 4$, $0 + 4 - 8 = -4$. Minimum $-4$.

**Answer: −4**

prompt: Alan, Ben and Craig, who have three distinct ages, are among five children running a race. Assuming there are no ties, in how many different orders can the five children finish the race with Alan, Ben and Craig in order from oldest to youngest?

solutions.title: Choose positions
solutions.body:
Choose which 3 of the 5 finishing places go to Alan, Ben and Craig: $\binom53 = 10$ ways; they must fill them in the one required order. The other two children fill the remaining 2 places in $2! = 2$ ways. Total $10 \times 2 = 20$.

**Answer: 20 orders**

solutions.title: Symmetry
solutions.body:
There are $5! = 120$ finishing orders. The three boys appear in each of their $3! = 6$ relative orders equally often, so exactly $\frac{120}{6} = 20$ have them oldest to youngest.

**Answer: 20 orders**

prompt: Let a *trime* be defined as a three-digit integer for which any two digits of the integer, ordered as they appear in the original integer, form a two-digit prime number. For example, 137 is a trime because 13, 17 and 37 are all prime numbers. However, 211 is not a trime because 21 is not prime. What is the greatest trime?

solutions.title: Search from the top
solutions.body:
For a trime $\overline{abc}$, the numbers $\overline{ab}$, $\overline{ac}$, $\overline{bc}$ are all prime, so $b$ and $c$ are odd and not 5.
- $a = 9$: the only prime in the 90s is 97, so $b = c = 7$, but 77 is not prime.
- $a = 8$: primes 83, 89 force $b, c \in \{3, 9\}$ with $\overline{bc}$ prime; 33, 39, 93, 99 are all composite.
- $a = 7$: primes 71, 73, 79. Try $b = 9$: $c \in \{1,3,9\}$ needs $\overline{9c}$ prime — none. Try $b = 3$: $c = 9$ gives 39 (no), $c = 3$ gives 33 (no), $c = 1$ gives 31 ✓. So 731 works (73, 71, 31 are prime).

**Answer: 731**

prompt: William counted all the animals he saw at the zoo. This graph shows the data he collected. Based on this, what percentage of the animals that William saw are mammals? Express your answer to the nearest hundredth.
How many ways are there to arrange the four integers 1, 2, 3 and 4 in a row so that no two adjacent numbers have a sum of 5?

solutions.title: Inclusion–exclusion
solutions.body:
The forbidden neighbors are $\{1,4\}$ and $\{2,3\}$. Of the $4! = 24$ arrangements, those with 1 and 4 adjacent: treat them as a block, $3! \cdot 2 = 12$. Likewise 12 with 2 and 3 adjacent. Both blocks: $2! \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 8$. Bad: $12 + 12 - 8 = 16$, good: $24 - 16 = 8$.

**Answer: 8 ways**

solutions.title: Build directly
solutions.body:
Start with 1: its neighbor can’t be 4, so the next is 2 or 3. 1-2-?: next can’t be 3, so 4, then 3: 1243. 1-3-?: next can’t be 2, so 4, then 2: 1342. So 2 arrangements start with 1; by symmetry 2 start with each digit: $4 \times 2 = 8$.

**Answer: 8 ways**

prompt: There are 93 sixth graders and 108 seventh graders entering a raffle. In each grade, the number of dog owners is twice the number of students who do not own a dog. What is the probability that a seventh grader who does not own a dog wins the raffle? Express your answer as a common fraction.

solutions.title: Count the group
solutions.body:
In seventh grade, $\frac13$ of students don’t own a dog: $108 \div 3 = 36$. There are $93 + 108 = 201$ entrants, so the probability is $\frac{36}{201} = \frac{12}{67}$.

**Answer: $\frac{12}{67}$**

prompt: In the $5 \times 5$ grid shown, each row and each column is to contain the integers 1 through 5 exactly once with one integer per cell. The sum of the two integers in each outlined pair of cells is 5. What is the product of the integers in the four corner cells that are shaded?

solutions.title: Fill the grid
solutions.body:
Each outlined pair is $\{1,4\}$ or $\{2,3\}$, so 5 never appears in a pair. Label cells (row, column) from the top left.

1. Row 5 has 3 in the corner, so its left pair is $\{1,4\}$; the remaining cells (5,3), (5,4) are 2 and 5. Cell (5,4) is in a pair, so it is 2 and (5,3) = 5; its partner (4,4) = 3.
2. Column 4 now has 3 and 2, so the pair (1,4)-(2,4) is $\{1,4\}$ and (3,4) = 5. Row 2 already has 1, so (2,4) = 4 and (1,4) = 1.
3. Row 2 then needs 2, 3, 5: the pair (2,2)-(2,3) is $\{2,3\}$ and (2,5) = 5. Column 3 has 2 at top, so (2,3) = 3, (2,2) = 2.
4. Column 5 has 1, 3, 5, so (1,5), (4,5) are 2, 4; row 1 has 2, so (1,5) = 4 and (4,5) = 2.
5. Row 3 has 5 and 1, so the pair (3,3)-(4,3) is (4, 1).
6. Column 1 has 1 in row 2, so (5,1) = 4 and (5,2) = 1. Row 1 needs 3 and 5 in (1,1), (1,2); row 4 needs 4 and 5 in (4,1), (4,2). Column 1 already has 4, so (4,1) = 5, which forces (1,1) = 3.

Corners: $3 \cdot 4 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 = 144$.

**Answer: 144**

prompt: A satellite, located 400 km above Earth’s surface, travels at a speed of 28,000 km/h. For simplicity, assume that Earth is a perfect sphere with circumference 40,075 km. How many minutes does it take the satellite to orbit Earth one time? Express your answer as a decimal to the nearest tenth.

solutions.title: Orbit circumference
solutions.body:
Increasing a circle’s radius by 400 km increases its circumference by $2\pi \cdot 400 \approx 2513.3$ km. The orbit is about $40{,}075 + 2513.3 = 42{,}588.3$ km long. Time: $\frac{42{,}588.3}{28{,}000} \approx 1.52101$ h $\times 60 \approx 91.3$ minutes.

**Answer: 91.3 minutes**

solutions.title: Via the radius
solutions.body:
Earth’s radius is $\frac{40{,}075}{2\pi} \approx 6378.1$ km, so the orbit radius is $\approx 6778.1$ km and its circumference $\approx 2\pi \cdot 6778.1 \approx 42{,}588$ km. At 28,000 km/h this takes $\approx 91.3$ minutes.

**Answer: 91.3 minutes**

prompt: Three children each live in one of three houses, equally spaced and arranged as shown. Each child is equally likely to live in any of the houses, and it is possible that a house has no children living in it. All three children will play in the house that minimizes the total distance they have to travel. What is the probability that they will play in house B?

solutions.title: Count the complement
solutions.body:
There are $3^3 = 27$ equally likely assignments. The best house is the one where the median child lives. They play at A exactly when at least two children live in A: all three in A (1 way) or exactly two ($3 \cdot 2 = 6$ ways), 7 in total. Likewise 7 for C. So house B is chosen in $27 - 14 = 13$ cases: probability $\frac{13}{27}$.

**Answer: $\frac{13}{27}$**

solutions.title: Count directly
solutions.body:
B is chosen when the median child is in B: either at least two children live in B ($1 + 3 \cdot 2 = 7$ ways), or exactly one lives in each house ($3! = 6$ ways). Total $13$ of 27.

**Answer: $\frac{13}{27}$**
